utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you please have the accused brought in. As far as I can see, he's not in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. I received yesterday after the hearing a waiver, so I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, for the record, could you please tell us what's happening with General Krstic, why he cannot be present today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, General Krstic is having certain health problems. The Chamber has already been informed of the nature of his health problems, and today he has a checkup at hospital. So for these reasons, for reasons of health, he waived his right to be here and provided the registry with the relevant document. He agreed that the proceedings continue in his absence, but I hope that he will be able to join us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Let me just bid you good morning, to the technicians, the interpreters, to the counsel. Good morning to Professor Radinovic. Professor Radinovic, you will continue to testify under oath. I will give the floor to Mr. Visnjic to continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Radinovic, yesterday we spoke about a certain level of independence in the chain of command of the Security Service. Could you tell the Chamber whether during your research you have ever come across a report which would have been sent by the security organ to the Commander of the unit that it belongs to; not to its superior command, but to the Commander of the unit in which composition it has found itself and which report would deal with the problem of the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I haven't come across a single document issued by the security organ during my preparations for this testimony, any document which would contain a report or information to the Superior Commander, either of the relevant brigade or the Drina Corps, about the assignment which the security organ was carrying out. Not only did I not find anything about their obligations within the chain of command of the Drina Corps, I also haven't come across any report issued by the security organ and sent upwards through the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would it have been conceivable for the Drina Corps officers and the Commander of the support units not to know about possible crimes committed by their members?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is conceivable for reasons contained in my answer to your previous question. That is to say, it was perfectly possible for the members of the military police of the brigades of the Drina Corps under the leadership of the assistant Commander for security in those brigades, that they were carrying out assignments which were outside the control of the Brigade Commander. Second reason for that could have been the fact that the Brigade Commanders and the command system of the Drina Corps as well were not informed, were not familiar with the conduct of the security organs; and that the Commanders and commanding officers, it would have been possible for them to think that their members were carrying out legal duties which did not involve cases of murder and burial. If I may add one further sentence, please, to support my claim. It was possible for this chain of command which was independent and which was not under the control of the usual, the normal command system of the Drina Corps, to use the resources of the brigades for certain activities involving the treatment of the prisoners of war. And it was possible for the Commanders to think that it was a legal activity and that murders, killings, and burials were not part of such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what was the responsibility of General Krstic for parts of that chain of command of the security elements in the period of time when crimes were committed, where mass killings were perpetrated in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, that is, up until the 18th or the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, General Krstic was at his post of the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps and the Commander of the Operational Group for planning, preparation, and execution of the Zepa operation. As such, he did not have the security organ of the corps in his control. They were not subordinate to him. And as a chief of staff, he did not have authority to exert control over that chain of command and control. Therefore, General Krstic cannot be held responsible for the acts and deeds of that particular chain of command because that fell out of his competence in his capacity of Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps and the Commander of the Operational Group for Zepa. Of course, this answer is truthful if similar things did not occur in the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, in view of the military doctrine, is the procedure of bringing in the prisoners of war in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade in the period from the 13th until the 11th of July -- until the 18th of July, is that understandable? Is that acceptable in the sense of the military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is completely contrary to the military doctrine for several reasons. Prisoners of war, in accordance with the principles of the military doctrine, are not held for a lengthy period of time in combat zones but are sent to collection centres that are provided for that purpose beforehand. The VRS had such a centre at the time. It was in Bijeljina at Batkovic. In view of the fact that in the orders of the Main Staff issued to the Drina Corps and in view of the fact that the Drina Corps was ordered to send the prisoners of war to the higher levels of command, it was unnecessary for the prisoners of war to be relocated, to be pulled out from the combat area and to be accommodated in a properly and adequately controlled collection centre. So that is one reason, and it has to do with the adopted norms and standards. The second reason is of a doctrinary nature. It is completely understandable. It cannot be conceived why the prisoners of war, at the time of the most intense fighting in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, were collected, were gathered in the area of responsibility of that brigade. Another doctrinary reason is the reason why those prisoners of war were put up in the area of the Zvornik Brigade when that area of responsibility in the overall area of responsibility of the Drina Corps is the most restricted one. There's less than 15 or 20 kilometres between the line of contact and the Drina River. So that portion of the area of responsibility was -- it was possible to cut that area of responsibility in two in cases of major attack from the direction of Tuzla. So militarily speaking, that would have caused a problem in respect of the prisoners of war. Those collection centres could have been deblocked, and I really don't know why such a situation occurred because what happened is completely contrary to the military doctrine. The only reason, the only explanation that could possibly be considered as rational was the fact that that particular area contained the highest number of facilities which could be used for the accommodation of prisoners of war and where it was possible, for a certain limited period of time, to control the prisoner of war with a relatively restricted number of resources. There are such possibilities outside this area, outside the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. There are several villages, but there are not enough adequate facilities for that. However, once again I have to say that all military reasons were contrary to that, that it was done contrary to military principles, military doctrinary principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to the testimonies that we have heard in this case, most of the executions were conducted in the area of deployment of certain battalions of the Zvornik Brigade. How can you comment on that proximity as regards a potential responsibility of the Commanders and their ability to learn about such executions and to do something about them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of these events, as far as I could learn from the material and the documents that I had access to while I was preparing for this testimony, combat activities were going on in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, and such combat activities were of a rather high intensity; that is, on the 14th, the 15th, the 16th, and the 17th of July, the area saw a rather high-intensity fighting. According to certain operational reports of the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade sent to the Commander of the Drina Corps, I came across information indicating that the intensity of combat activities from the area of Tuzla, from the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps of the BiH army, was very high. Why am I saying this? It was possible for the shots -- it was possible for the Commanders of those battalions not to identify the shots coming from the executions as something unexpected. That could not have been the reason for them being upset or concerned about it and induced to ask reasons for such shooting, because shots are not uncommon and the noise from firing is not uncommon in area of high combat activities. It's not a justification; it's a mere fact. The second fact which goes to the issue of the command responsibility of the Battalion Commanders, in view of the principles of the military doctrine which was in force in the VRS and which had been adopted from the JNA, battalions in defensive action, as were the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade, are not assigned a particular area of responsibility as is the case with the brigades. A battalion is only assigned to deploy in a region of defence, as it is called, and such regions have two positions: the front position and the rear position. And it also includes firing positions of the firing group of the battalion. And they have their command post, the battalion command post, but it is a very restricted area, very restricted terrain. It's merely a spot in such an area. The difference between a brigade and a battalion is the fact that every battalion is assigned a region of defence which contains two separate parts, two lines, two lines of facilities which they have to take possession of, and is not assigned a particular area of responsibility which it is supposed to control and have responsibility for. So that is the specific difference between battalions and brigades. Second, battalions of the Zvornik Brigade and the battalions of the Drina Corps and the VRS in general, as is the case with all of the three armies in the BiH, are not very strong. They do not have a high number of troops, unlike Western battalions which have -- which can have between 800 and 1.000 troops. The number of troops in these battalions was 2 to 300, so they were not able to take control of the features as part of their defence which would secure them such a portion of the terrain which is described by the military doctrine. And the military doctrine which was applicable in the VRS provided for the battalion to take possession of the territory which is 3 kilometres wide and 1.5 to 2 kilometres long. So it was very difficult for these, these type of battalions to cover such a large area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, yesterday you explained to the Trial Chamber the existence of several individual systems of command in the zone of the Drina Corps. Was it realistic to expect that the Drina Corps, or rather, that the system of command of the Drina Corps could function successfully and control all the events that were taking place and activities that were taking place in their zone of responsibility in July 1995? Was that realistic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all in answer to your question, let me say what this should have been like in principle; what the principle of the matter should have been. The command of the Drina Corps had to ensure an insight into the situation as it existed and prevailed in the zone of responsibility. It had to do so according to doctrinary principles. It would have had to have done so. In the zone of responsibility, nothing could take place which the command system of the Drina Corps was not in control of. So that is the principle as it stands. Now, from that principle, which is a normal requirement and would be normal to expect, going down to practice itself and the actual situation on the ground as it is and was, is a subject for analysis. We can debate the point. Yesterday I spoke about several systems of leadership in that zone which functioned simultaneously and upon which the command system of the Drina Corps did not -- it was not possible for it to establish control over it either de facto or in normative terms. So at the same time, we saw the functioning of systems, the simultaneous functioning of systems over which the Drina Corps, by nature of the position in military hierarchy, did not wield any influence on nor could it wield any influence on. Therefore, on the command system of Superior Command, it was not able to exert any influence. The second point I would like to stress here is that in the zone of possibility of the Drina Corps we saw the units and compositions active which belonged to those various and different command systems upon which the Drina Corps could not exert any influence, and they were, as we saw yesterday, the units under the immediate direct command of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and the units which were under the direct command of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Republika Srpska. So the Drina Corps exerted -- did not exert -- not only did it not -- was it not able to establish control over these units nor could it have done because by virtue of the documents and orders it was not organised to do so nor was it duty-bound to do so. This was not mandatory. The command system of the Drina Corps vis-a-vis those systems which were not under its control and which it could not control were duty-bound that having learnt of what had happened to have undertaken the steps which are provided for and prescribed for in the rules of service for the VRS and relate to the execution of orders. That means the duty and obligation of each and every person to undertake proceedings that all illegal acts which took place in the zone of responsibility must be -- that the long arm of the law must come to persecute them. The next reason which could have led to something that was natural to expect, that is to say that the Drina Corps could control the situation in its zone of responsibility, the next factor that did not allow it to do so was the confusion that resulted from the simultaneous complicated conditions and factors that prevailed on the ground; namely, the danger of seeing a breakthrough into the zone of responsibility along the Tuzla-Zvornik axis at the time, that is to say, between the 15th to the 17th, and prior to that as well, from the 14th onwards. That serious crisis came to a head in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. The second fact which influenced this general confusion was the problem of preventing the withdrawal of the 28th Division to break through the zone of responsibility. And third, the third reason which led to this operational operative confusion in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps was that a large portion of the resources of the corps was deployed and used at the Zepa operation, and that was an operation which was being launched in a completely separate portion of the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps. This, therefore, led the fact that the command system focused -- of the Drina Corps focused on solving these operational problems which came to a head at that time and were very serious. In other words, the military system of command was focused on operational problems, that is to say, it tried to deal with the crises that took place in combat and in the activities at Zepa, whereas the other problems which are the subject of these legal proceedings was left to the other systems, the systems that existed in parallel form. And the Drina Corps had no influence exerted, no influence, or had any influence on those parallel systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have one question that I must ask you, General, if I may. Having heard your explanation here, which I understand in theoretical terms, I'm driven back, though, to one question. You yourself discussed at an earlier point the intercept which came back from Colonel Pandurevic of the Zvornik Brigade when he went back from Zepa down during the crisis. He was called back and then he sent an intercept and he talked about the problems of detention of 3.000 people being in some form of detention, 7.000 people coming in from the column, and he used the term, if I remember correctly, "I need" -- in effect, "I need more resources or I will have to let them go," which sounded very much the tone of the intercept was that he considered himself still as the head of the brigade to be dealing with the situation or to have to deal with the situation of the prisoners of war rather than what you postulated as a whole independent control system for the prisoners that he had no control over. I'm just wondering if you could, in your theory, put those two things together.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response -- that is to say, the first sentence of my response was that the Drina Corps had to establish control over the zone of responsibility, would have had to. That was its duty and obligation and that is incontestable, without a doubt. The report, the intercept that you talk about, I think was dated the 18th of July; that is to say that there are two reports. One was on the 18th of July, the second on the 15th of July. So as soon as the report came from Zepa, the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade in the interim combat report stated that an additional problem was the prisoners. The prisoners were an additional problem for him, whom somebody had brought into his zone of responsibility; whereas the appeal which speaks about the 3.000 prisoners of war and 7.000 others in the woods, I think that refers to the 18th of July, that the date there was the 18th of July, but I'm not quite sure. I think that is so. And that is, for me, completely incontestable, that is to say that the command of the Zvornik Brigade when sending out those reports did not know that -- of the liquidation of the prisoners of war in his zone of responsibility because it was quite obvious that at the time that he was reporting on this, these prisoners of war, according to the documentation that I had at my disposal for preparing for this testimony, that fact about the prisoners was not in Zvornik. So it is evident that the Commander did not know about that fact, and if he did not know about that fact, that is an indication for me that he did not control that system. Why didn't he control the system? He didn't control the system because the problem of prisoners of war, by virtue of its very nature and the internal function of command, is something that the Security Service deals with, as can be concluded from the orders of the Commanders at all levels of command. And that problem on the division of work in the Zvornik Brigade belonged to the assistant Commander for security and the platoon of the military police. And it is quite certain that his assistant for security and the police probably knew about that at the time when this execution took place and the burials took place, but neither his security officer nor his police had to have -- at the beginning of this treatment of the prisoners knew that at the end of the chain, they would be executed. So I'm trying to explain how this could have happened, how this could have come about, of course without any apriori attempt to justify anything that happened in that chain. What I'm trying is for my angle of vision as a witness, as an expert witness, I am trying to see how that could have happened and how that could have been allowed to happen. I'm trying to make that clear to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions, but I do have a correction to make in the transcript for this last response by General Radinovic, and it is in line 7. General Radinovic mentioned just a report, not an intercept. He said "report," not "intercept," so the report is -- the "intercept" is wrong. And in line 10, General Radinovic did not talk about Zepa, so that word "Zepa" is not properly -- is not appropriate. And in line 3.000, he mentioned -- in line 13 he mentioned 3.000 prisoners. There was the figure "3" which had nothing to do with that. The figure was 3.000 prisoners. Those are my remarks with regard to the LiveNote, Mr. President, and my corrections. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Visnjic. I think that this would be an opportune moment to take a break, perhaps, before we start with the cross-examination. Mr. Cayley, is that convenient?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you wish, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a 20-minute break, after which we will start the cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Radinovic, you will now be answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor, and in this case it is Mr. Cayley who will be asking you the questions. Mr. Cayley, your witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, my name is Cayley. I'm from the Office of the Prosecutor, and I will be asking you questions on your evidence. And let me say to you from the outset --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, you can intervene if there is anything here that I say which is out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- you've given your evidence in-chief, and it's been in a very long narrative form where you've been very expansive in what you have said. My questions should elicit from you fairly short responses. Not every question can be answered by yes and no, and I understand that, and of course you will be given every opportunity by the Judges to make sure that you can give a full response; but we have got a lot of material to get through in a limited period of time, so if you could tailor your response to my question, that would be very helpful. Is that clear, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall answer in keeping with the knowledge I have of the facts related to the case and in keeping with my temperament, of course, because there is a component part of my psychological makeup. So anything that is not forbidden to me by the Trial Chamber I shall do, but I will, of course, try to adhere to your requests, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you have your report to hand?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could turn to page 10 of your report, and it is in fact page 11 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This document has not yet been given an exhibit number, although I do think my learned friend is probably offering it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Apparently, Mr. Visnjic, I'm sorry, it's been given a Prosecutor's exhibit number, 755.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that seems to be a rather strange marking in view of the fact that it is a Defence exhibit. But I would just like to indicate that the General has his report before him, but that this time his report is in a different version, that is to say, the pages will not coincide. So perhaps the registry can provide him with the same version of his report so as to overcome that technical difficulty. So may we just wait a few moments for the General to get the same copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In -- excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but there seems to be a conflict here. Now, the Prosecution and the Defence seems to want this document for themselves. Now, how do we stand there? Because it has already been marked for identification but not admitted yet, so I think the Defence ought to be given preference here because it is, after all, a report by their expert witness. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, you're absolutely right. Mr. Harmon has thousands of very efficient people working for him upstairs who put numbers on everything the moment they see a document, so it should have a Defence exhibit number on it. It's not our report. I think it was done in haste because the Defence hadn't actually offered it into evidence, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. One must be careful, otherwise, Mr. Harmon risks getting a number too himself. Now the Defence is going to tender that document into evidence. Is that correct, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President, and I can provide a number for purposes of the record. It would be Defence Exhibit D160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, is that right? Is that the proper number for that document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have two blank spaces, D159 -- yes, one space, D159, but you may already have an exhibit labelled D159, do you, that you did not submit yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we leave it at number D160 and then we'll fill in D159 as we go along in due course?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this document will be document D160, 1-6-0, for purposes of identification. So when we refer to the document, we can refer to it in that fashion. Mr. Cayley, without further ado, I think we can proceed. General Radinovic has the proper version before him, the pages coincide with your own copy, so I think we can proceed, Mr. Cayley. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, if you could turn to page 10 of your report, which I think deals with the sources that you used for your report. Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying that as far as your primary sources are concerned, you were given access by the Defence to all of the Prosecution and Defence exhibits which are in evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is, but I can't say for sure. I can't give you a precise answer, but I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic may be able to clarify this later, but we'll carry on with the cross-examination for the moment. You did have access to radio intercepts of VRS forces, did you not? And in fact, you refer to them in your list of primary sources.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had access, but I did not use them as my primary source because for the type of expertise that I engage in, intercepts cannot be considered to be primary sources because we must know the strategic context in which they occurred, who the people speaking were, what functions they had, who they were talking to and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but may I finish what I was saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, we will actually get on to discuss the quality of the intercepts later on in your examination in chief and you will be able to say everything you want to say about intercepts. For the moment, all I want to do is to specifically identify what you used and what you didn't use in compiling this report. Can you read out from the paragraph that has listed primary Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sources. Could you read out the final sentence after the semicolon which reads "Tribunal documents given with the indictment"? Could you read that please, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Tribunal documents given with the indictment, intercepted conversations, tables and diagrams, maps and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That sentence is contained within which is the paragraph headed up "Primary sources," is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you did use intercept as a primary source in your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the extent to which I considered them to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in respect of secondary sources, you included there "thematic studies relating to the problem of operation Srebrenica and the events after its termination." Now, I think you used, did you not, Radovan Karadzic's book that was written by Dejan Lukic called "My Defence", did you not? Did you refer to that book in your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm not going to put this into evidence, but this is in fact the book. How heavily did you rely on this particular book?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you read the chapters on Srebrenica? There are two chapters, aren't there, I think, which concern Srebrenica and what happened and the aftermath of Srebrenica? Did you read these two chapters?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to read all of that book, but I'm just going to read on the back of this book what it says. Mr. Karadzic says, on the back of this particular publication, which I think Mr. Lukic has quoted: "My plea at The Hague would be an accusation rather than a defence. It is Lords, Secretaries-General, presidents, and ministers of sorts who should turn up there and come out into open."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not hear the question put by Mr. Cayley. I don't understand whether the expert witness is asked to comment on the stand taken by President Karadzic, or whether it was just -- whether he had read that portion of the book. If he said that he was acquainted with the book, then it is certain that he read that part; but if he is being asked to comment on what Radovan Karadzic says in that book in that portion, I don't know whether that comes within the domain of his expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that Mr. Cayley has asked his question yet. Shall we wait and see what the actual question is, Mr. Visnjic? Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, what do you think Mr. Karadzic meant when he said that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not here to interpret Karadzic. He could have thought what he liked. So that -- I did not pay specific attention to that part of his text, but if you want me to tell you what I think about it, then may I have a copy and I shall read through it and then be able to tell you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This, unfortunately, is an English version, General. I assume you read it in the Serbian version which I don't have to hand, but if we do refer to this book later on, I will indeed give you a copy in your own language if we refer to the two chapters which you have referred to in your report, which you have relied on to some extent in your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for having to add the following. It's not an answer to the question, but let me just say that when you -- if you wish to ask me about things like that, you must give me the possibility of reading through the portion again. I have read many books, and I can't be expected to remember sections of individual books. But I have nothing against giving my judgement and saying what I think about what you're asking me, but I would have had to have read through the section first. So please provide me with that possibility if you want me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, have no fear, any documents that we look at in detail, you will have copies placed in front of you. What other books did you rely on for your report, other than the Karadzic book? Just give a list.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony and in answer to questions from the Defence, I think I spoke about that in greater detail, and I think it exists in the transcript. I studied a number of books by Muslim authors. I think that one of them was Nesib Mandzic, that that was his name. Then there was Masic, Sefer Halilovic. That is as my memory serves me. Those three quite certainly, but I couldn't give you the names of the others at present. So of the Muslim authors, I read those three books. I also read the book that you have just mentioned by Dejan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in terms of actors in these events who were from the International Community, did you read the book by Carl Bildt?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "A Mission of Peace," I have read it, and I think I quoted it in my report. And from the whole series of books, that was the last one I read so that my recollections of that book are freshest in my mind, although I did have problems in accepting everything that he sets out and in recalling it all because it's not a very well-ordered book, if you don't mind my saying that. It is not the kind of text that I'm accustomed to read; that is to say, it hasn't got a firm structure where you can see the thesis, the arguments, and the conclusions. So it was a little difficult for me to follow because it was more the type of publication that is more lax. It is not very rigid in its demands and strict in its demands, but I do think that I remember the basic points and thesis put forward in the book, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just literally in the form of a shopping list - you don't need to give your opinion on every book - which other books did you read, if you can recall, published by members of the International Community who were involved in these events? Were there any others?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the report by the Secretary-General, by Michael Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The report of the Secretary-General, you mean the report by Kofi Annan; and I think when you're referring to Michael Rose, you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And when you're referring to Michael Rose, you're referring to General Sir Michael Rose who is the Commander of UNPROFOR forces who wrote a book on Bosnia. You read that book as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read that book, that is to say, excerpts of it. The excerpts were published in our newspapers and journals, so that is why I did not quote it in my report as a source. It would be difficult for me to refer back to the book at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I want you to think about the VRS orders that you looked at. Now, you would agree with me that neither you nor I have had sight of every single Bosnian Serb army order that was issued in respect of the events with which this Court is concerned.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have managed to look through what I had at my disposal for these legal proceedings, what I received from the Defence as documents, the ones that are considered to be relevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that there are -- that the sum total of what the Defence and the Prosecution have in their possession are not all of the written orders that were, in fact, issued in respect of the events with which the Court is concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me questions which I cannot answer. For me to be able to answer your question, I would have to know how many documents were actually in existence, and then to subtract from that number the number of documents I had at my disposal, and then I would know whether I had omitted to study some of the documents. I can only assume that they exist, but I cannot give you a clear-cut answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I'm not asking you to give me the numbers of the missing documents. Let me just state to you that the Office of the Prosecutor has been seeking a large number of orders, written orders, that are relevant to these proceedings for some considerable time, and those proceedings are ongoing. And I will just refer to one particular request which was requested to Branko Milosevic who is the liaison officer for Republika Srpska in Banja Luka. I won't read the letter, but in that letter, at the end of November of this year we request orders in respect of the Drina Corps, the Drina Corps Chief of Security, the Drina Corps Chief of Logistics, the Milici Brigade, the Vlasenica Brigade, the 5th Engineering Battalion, and we give dates of all of the orders and reports that we want that are relevant to these proceedings. The response from the Defence Ministry of Republika Srpska, on the 15th of February, 2000, was simply an explanation that many of these documents have disappeared or were, in fact, destroyed when the government changed. Are you aware that many of the documents that are relevant to these proceedings have, in fact, disappeared? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I did not know that the relevant documents had disappeared nor that they had been destroyed. If they were destroyed and if they did disappear, then I can understand that. I can understand that because it is -- it is the kind of thing that happens during the kind of war that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I don't know of a single civil war where things like that don't happen. Documents are not registered in the way they should be, war diaries, archives are not kept, and documents are not stored in the professional way. That is understandable to me. Now, the scope of those documents that were destroyed, how many of them and how relevant they were, I really don't know. I really can't say. But I do believe that I did have relevant documents at my disposal on the basis of which it is possible, with relative measure of certainty, to reconstruct what had taken place in the events that we are discussing at this trial. And, of course, it is up to the person deciding to assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you'd agree with me that there will have been oral orders issued during these events which neither you nor I are aware of?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the right of the command system to issue oral commands, especially in current events, ongoing events. But I, as a military expert, can assume that such things happened but I cannot base my testimony on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, the first 15 or so pages of your report are concerned with historical events going back to, I think, the sixteenth century and the Ottoman Empire, and I'm not going to ask you any questions about that at all. Let us move straight to the twentieth century. Now, my understanding is that the essence of your testimony concerning the Serbs of Bosnia is that they wished to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and when it became clear that that was impossible, they wanted to create a Serb political entity within Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite correct. If you wish for me to respond precisely to this question, you must give me the opportunity to formulate my answer. So I cannot answer by yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't expect yes or no, but briefly, briefly, because this is not the heart of the case. But if you can briefly, in about the same amount of time as my question, answer that, that would be perfect?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not as skilful as you are in order to reply so briefly, but the first fact that should be kept in mind is that for the creation of Yugoslavia in 1918 and for the creation of Yugoslavia in 1941, the Serbs or the Serbian people, which at that time numbered between 6 million and 7 million, spent or lost 3 million people. Three million Serbs were killed. And the political programme was the formation of a common state of southern Slavs and that programme was drafted a long time ago. The second fact that I would like you to keep in mind is that the people who had such major sacrifices for the creation of such a state spent vast national energy in order to preserve it because that state enabled them all to live in the same state. This was the first time in history that all Serbs lived in one state in Yugoslavia, and they were really willing to defend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1990. I'm talking about this civil war, the war that this court is dealing with. I'm not talking about the history that preceded it. If you can't answer the question without giving a historical analysis going back to the beginning of the century, we'll move ahead. Now, I --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't allow me to answer your question. Serbs in Bosnia did want to preserve that state and for Bosnia-Herzegovina as their state to be within Yugoslavia. So the political programme was that. So thanks to the supremacy of the political forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina this concept was not accepted, but they opted for the complete separation of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia. So the breaking up again of the Serbian people into sections which would remain in Serbia and sections which would remain within other republics of that once common state, then the political programme of the political leaders of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina was for Bosnia-Herzegovina to be reconstituted as a community of all three peoples which would all be equal and constitutive parts of the state. So the programme which was closest to this idea was the so-called Cutiliero Plan. He is a Portuguese diplomat who proposed that Bosnia be a confederation based on a cantonal principle, and the leaders of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina accepted that concept. Under whose incitement or how this happened, the already-accepted plan was rejected by leaders of the Muslim community. So they rejected Cutiliero's plan. So according to my view and according to what I know, this served as an introduction for the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Later on there were other factors that attributed to this, but politically speaking, this was one of the basic causes for this conflict. So I'm really speaking about this subject in quite an analytical manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I think on the 6th of March, 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina held a referendum and voted to be a sovereign state; is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Bosnia and Herzegovina but members of the Muslim and Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbian people did not participate in this referendum. In the prior constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina they were a constitutive people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the referendum without the participation of one of the constitutional peoples is not a legitimate one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm right in saying that on the 7th of March the United States of America and the European Community, the then European Community, now the European Union, recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state. This is a matter of public record, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a generally accepted fact. This was on April 7th, not March.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misspoke. You're quite right. But it occurred on the 7th of April, 1992, the event that I've just stated?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 746.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a document which is signed by the president of the Serbian National Assembly in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 12th of May, 1992, and it sets out the strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is one paragraph that I'm interested in and the only one that I wish to discuss with you. It sets out on this document the aims of the Serbian people, but paragraph 3 says to: "Establish a corridor in the Drina river valley, that is, eliminate the Drina as a border separating Serbian States." Now, that area, General, if I'm right, incorporates the Podrinje region which you said was for the Serbs the "to be or not to be" part of a Serb area within Bosnia; is that right? To use your words. I think you quoted Shakespeare, Hamlet.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't quote, I used that metaphor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But am I right in saying that the Podrinje area is within this area referred to in paragraph 3 of this decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is not Podrinje, this is Drina. This is a historical concept since King Theodosious divided the kingdom to his sons and the kingdom was divided into the eastern and western part. Unfortunately for the Serbian people, it divides the Serbian ethnic space into two parts, the western and the eastern part. And in this decision, in this document that you have pointed me to, the political leaders of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina believed that it is a legitimate aim for this pointer not to pass through the very centre of their territory but for this border to be moved. These are quite desirable political objectives. Many objectives perhaps cannot be carried out, but if you wish, this for me something that is quite normal. Podrinje is along this border.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So in your evidence when you said that without Central Bosnia the Serbs could not form a political entity , that area, Podrinje, includes Bratunac, Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba, Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the translation of your question I heard "Central Bosnia." I think probably there is a mistake in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Central Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In my response to the question by the Defence, I spoke about the strategic significance of that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina for all three sides in the conflict, and I said, and I am replying to you now, that none of the three warring sides had such a major interest in Central Podrinje as the Serbian side did, because without Podrinje, you cannot have a political entity of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think this is the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, let's move straight to the summer of 1992, and I want to ask you if you are aware of certain events that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, Mr. Usher, Prosecutor's Exhibit 485 could be placed on the board next to the General. Let's not waste the time. Can you just lean it up against the board?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, at about the same time as the declaration that we've just looked at by Mr. Krajisnik about creating a corridor in the Drina River valley, certain events were taking place in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Prosecutor's Exhibit 37 could be made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is a document unfortunately which is in English, but I'm going to quote some sections to you from it - not all of it, very briefly - and I just want to know whether or not you were aware that these events were taking place. This report, General, is a report by an individual by the name of Tadeusz Mazowiecki who was appointed by the United Nations in 1993 to produce a report on human rights, alleged human rights abuses in Eastern Bosnia. It is a document which I'm sure was made available to you. Even if you didn't read it, it's a document the Defence had. Now, this particular report describes events in the town of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, excuse me. Mr. Visnjic, one has to bear something in mind. If you have an objection as regards the transcript, that's fine. If you have an objection to the question of the Prosecutor, you have to let him finish his question. Proceed with your objection for this time, but let me remind you once again that only when you have pertinent objections can we hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection for the use of this document. Defence received this document in the English version. It was never translated, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I'm sorry, but it is the witness who can tell us that. The Prosecutor has said, "You have perhaps seen the document. It is in the English language." The witness can say yes or no. He can tell us whether he has had the document, whether he has had it in English and was unable to read it. You have to leave the witness the opportunity to respond to the question. I think that the witness is also aware of the problem and that he will let us know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, this is a document which is in English. Have you seen this document that's in front of you? Can you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I realise you're at a disadvantage because you cannot read it, and I won't spend very long with this particular document. It refers strictly to events that were taking place that were reported on by Mr. Mazowiecki to the UN, and all I want you to do is to cast your memory back to 1992 and 1993 and recall for the Judges whether or not you can remember these particular events taking place. Let me read the report, and the report is titled "Ethnic Cleansing of the Eastern Enclaves." "The first wave of ethnic cleansing in Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina was carried out by Serb forces in April and May of 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is at the bottom of page 3, Mr. Usher, and then it goes over the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "Only three pockets or enclaves remained under government control in the east. For most of this period the enclaves consisted of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa." There is then a description in the main body of the report about the siege of the Cerska area, the Cerska Valley which can be seen on the map. I won't read it, but essentially a large number of civilians were surrounded by Serbian forces and subjected to shelling and siege-like conditions for many months. Were you aware of these events in Cerska in the summer of 1992, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew from the media. I knew that from the media, not from documents; but since I know that the media tend to exaggerate, I had sufficient reason not to wholly believe in the facts that were published by the media. But certainly in the war which started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and since I know what civil wars look like, that type of activity and that type of consequences are quite expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in your own evidence, General, you then refer to a government offensive, a Bosnian government offensive from December of 1992 to January of 1993, and you discussed in that the fall of the village of Kravica and the killing of a number of Serbs. And indeed, that particular event is also referred to in this report, although unfortunately due to lack of cooperation of the Serbian authorities, Mr. Mazowiecki was only able to essentially write these in the forms of allegations, but those events are referred to. Now, moving on, you then stated in your evidence, and do you recall this, that there was a Drina Corps offensive following on from the Bosnian government offensive in March of 1993 to retake ground taken by the Muslims. Do you remember saying that in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you have had opportunity --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Usher, this is Prosecutor's Exhibit number 30, which is the Secretary-General's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have had an opportunity to read this report, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999, yes, the report of the Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's correct. And you've read that in your own language?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do we have a copy of that in the Serbian language? I will read out the section concerned, if the relevant paragraph can be placed on the ELMO. This is paragraph 37. If the Defence has a copy to assist the witness, they can let the General have it so that he can follow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately we do not have a copy in the Serbian language, and it was never tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, I think that we have a translation service here, that is, the interpreters; and Mr. Cayley can read the relevant portion, and the General will receive the interpretation from the booth, and we will be able to follow it on the ELMO. Please continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, it's page 13 of the report, paragraph 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, it's a very short section within the report, and it refers to the following: "Bosniak forces attacked out of the enclave against the Serb inhabited village of Kravica on 7 January 1993. Serb sources claimed that over 40 Serb civilians were killed in the attack." That's what you referred to in your evidence, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next sentence, "Soon after the attack on Kravica, Serb forces began to prepare a counter-offensive." And here we're talking about the Drina Corps, aren't we, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "By March 1993, Serb forces were advancing rapidly, killing and burning as they did so." Would you agree with that characterisation, General, that the Secretary-General of the United Nations gives to the Serb counter-attack?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A fact is missing from this report of the Secretary-General and that is the fact that Kravica, Kravica is the last village in Central Podrinje which was inhabited by Serbs. And since then, from January 7th, and it's very symbolic and it's obvious because it's the Orthodox Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. You've already agreed with me about the attack on Kravica by Muslim forces and the allegations that Serbs were killed. What I'm asking you about, General, is the characterisation of the -- listen to me.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the last Serbian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This report, the second sentence, concerns the characterisation of the Serb counter-attack against the Muslims. Do you agree or disagree with that particular characterisation of that, whether the Drina Corps, in your words, "... advanced rapidly, killing and burning as they did so"? Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree that the Drina Corps advanced killing and burning. The Drina Corps, which carried out a counter-attack in Central Podrinje, was on the road along which the road was advancing, and the army was from that area, which was completely ethnically cleansed by the Muslims until the Orthodox Christmas of 1993. On that road, they found unburied corpses of their family members, of their household members, so the remains, the bodies, of their dearest ones. So, sir, unfortunately, previously all Serbian settlements had been ethnically cleansed and destroyed in Central Podrinje, and Kravica was only the sad epilogue of that previous cleansing. Before that, the cleansing was carried out in other areas which were under the control of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, to end this particular discussion, this report indicates that by March of 1993, the entire Muslim populations of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Vlasenica, Sadic, and Kamenica, were either all in the Srebrenica enclave or had fled to Tuzla, and that the population of Srebrenica had expanded from 7.000 to 60.000 people, including the surrounding villages. Are you aware of those facts? Did you hear about those facts during 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the information about such a number of citizen -- or such a number of the population in Srebrenica is not correct. I don't think that the town can accept that many people, but this is not really that important, the figure itself. But I agree with you that the concentration of population was much -- much exceeded the resources of the town in order to enable normal living.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, let's move forward rapidly to April of 1993 and a matter that you've discussed which was the protected area, the safe area, Resolution 819. And you also stated in your evidence that there was a military agreement between Mr. Mladic, General Mladic, and the then Commander of the Bosnian government forces. Do you recall referring to that agreement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you stated in your evidence that the Muslims essentially totally failed to respect that agreement over the next two years.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you also said that the Bosnian Serb army fully respected that agreement. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's just read through, and again, my apologies because it is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We're now back on Prosecutor's Exhibit 37, and it might be a good idea to actually place this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I will summarise the seven points of that agreement between the Serbs and the Muslims. The first part of the agreement, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a principled objection and I will not ask this question again, but I would like to make the following objection: When you are using a document which is not accessible to the witness in his language, I think that it is unnecessary to quote from such a document. Mr. Cayley can summarise the question and cite his source. But if he reads this and quotes from the document to the witness, I think we will lose a lot of time, and I'm not sure whether the witness can provide a good answer to the question since the whole document is not accessible to him. So this is a general objection to such questions. So if the witness has a translation of the document, it is possible to quote. But if not, then I think that the way I suggested would be appropriate and we would save much time and get on much faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, how do you respond to this objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. In this particular instance, that is exactly what I'll do. There may be documents which are not in the language of the witness which I will read. I mean, I'm reading it so that he can actually understand in his own language and so that I'm not mischaracterising what is actually contained in the document. That is the only risk. Indeed Your Honours have this document available to you to read. I mean, it's a huge document that's 20-odd pages of typed script. I'm not reading all of it. So I will do that in this instance. I'll summarise the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Cayley, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Page 9, at the bottom of the page. These are just, General, the elements of the military agreement that took place between the Muslims and the Serbs in respect to the safe area following on from Resolution 819, and if you could simply say yes or no in respect of the particular points of agreement, that would be helpful. Now, the first point of agreement was a total ceasefire between the parties, is that right, in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next requirement was the deployment of a company of UN Protection Force soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next requirement was the opening of an air corridor for the evacuation of the seriously wounded and ill to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next requirement was the demilitarisation of the enclave and the requirement that the Muslims hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next requirement was freedom of movement for both sides?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next requirement was freedom of movement for the International Community and the access of humanitarian aid into the city of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the final requirement was that prisoners be exchanged between the two parties. Now, General, are you aware that in -- I think it was April, 25th of April, 1993, the Secretary-General sent in a special representative to Srebrenica to make a report on what he found in the area. Mr. Diego Arria, who was the permanent representative of Venezuela, and he stated and I summarise that the Serbs were not complying with the military agreement because they had not withdrawn from points where they could attack, harass, or terrorise the town. Are you aware of the fact that the Serbs did not withdraw in accordance with the military agreement, the Bosnian Serb forces? Are you aware of that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should be familiar with the ways a particular area can be demilitarised in order to understand why Serbs didn't withdraw. In 1992, I took part in the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan in the Krajina region, and I was in charge of the disengagement of forces. The first omission of the agreement that you have just quoted was the fact that it did not contain at the time it was reached a defined boundary of the safe area. So the agreement did not contain a specific and articulated plan of demilitarisation. A demilitarisation plan should contain a full dysfunctioning process of putting out of function the Muslim forces in the enclave so that their military resources and equipment can be pulled out. In that way, the military situation would have been defused and the enclave would no longer be exposed to any danger. Since that was not specifically regulated in the agreement, that particular element had to be done subsequently and that was the reason -- that was why there were so many violations of the agreement which eventually led to the operation Srebrenica 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, are you aware that the Serbs systematically prevented humanitarian aid from 1993 through to June of 1995, they systematically prevented humanitarian aid from getting into the enclave of Srebrenica? And before you answer this question, the Judges have heard evidence both from the commanding officer of the Dutch Battalion who said that that's -- that is exactly what happened, and they have also seen UNMO reports which indicate that that happened. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably haven't heard the fact that the concept of humanitarian convoys was jeopardised because certain prohibited equipment was being brought into Srebrenica. I absolutely do not support the idea of holding up the convoys and preventing the aid to reach the civilian settlements. However, you must understand the reality of the situation, because on a number of occasions it was discovered that the convoys were carrying military equipment, weapons, ammunition, and other types of materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, General, in his evidence to the Court, refers to the fact that the Serbs, by April 1995, were not allowing food into the enclave, they were not allowing spare parts for his vehicles, for Dutch vehicles, they were not allowing Dutch personnel back into the enclave, and I won't read out all of his evidence, but he describes the effect of no food on a starving population. Are you aware, General, that this was taking place? Are you aware of these events?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard such testimonies. Whether that was indeed the case, I don't know. What I want to say is that I don't have any confirmation of the testimony of Colonel Karremans. However, let me assure you that the activities of the Dutch Battalion in respect of the control of the regime of the safe area and the conduct of all of the participants was inadequate and that there was enough reasons for the Serbian side not to abide strictly by the agreement but to control all entries to the safe area because such entries were detrimental to the overall regime of the safe area. And that attitude of the Serb side, that is that they were preventing entry of the humanitarian convoys into the area, was actually a consequence of the situation, and Colonel Karremans, who was at the head of the Dutch Battalion, was responsible for the violations of such a regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So by saying, General, that the Serbs did not strictly abide by the agreement, it's incorrect, isn't it, to say that the VRS fully respected the military agreement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this Chamber and on the basis of the document which was issued by the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the VRS, I showed what his order was in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, that is a very, very straightforward question. It links onto exactly what you've just said. You've just stated to this Court that the Serbs did not strictly comply with the military agreement that had been reached in respect of Resolution 819. On that basis, is it correct or incorrect that the VRS fully respected the agreement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed the attitude of the parties towards the agreement itself, and I told this Chamber that at the very beginning, the VRS took up a perfectly correct position, that is, that they were respecting, fully respecting the agreement from the beginning. On the other hand, the Muslim side violated the agreement at the very beginning, at the day it was supposed to enter into force, by not demilitarising the zone and by not handing over the weapons as was provided for in the agreement. In that way, both the system of the United Nations and the Muslim side --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- violated the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may. Can I put the question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Radinovic, if you have to start from the beginning for every single answer that you wish to give to the Prosecutor, this will take us nowhere. It will be far better for all of us for you to answer your questions briefly and clearly. But let me take advantage of this opportunity to ask you a question. At any point in time did the Serb authorities notify the United Nations of the violations of the agreement that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assumption is that they did. I know that it was publicly discussed. It was discussed at the meetings in which I took part that the violations were commonplace, that the agreement is not being ordered, from the demilitarised area Sabotage Units were being infiltrated into the rear of the Serb side and that that side suffered losses. I don't know how the command of the VRS could have complied strictly with the agreement in terms of complete freedom of movement in view of the fact that the regime inside of the zone itself was not respected. But the reality was, actually, that the safe area was militarily active. And I should like to stress the necessity of bearing that particular fact in mind when discussing these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to assess the general situation, one needs to proceed step-by-step. We will have enough time to do that, but let me now ask you once again to try and provide direct answers to the questions put to you by the Prosecutor. Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, just to briefly finish on this issue, Colonel Karremans, in his evidence, stated - and I think I may have said this to you already - that his personnel were prevented from returning to the enclave by Serb forces. Equipment, ammunition was all prevented from getting into the enclave and by Serb forces. Now, you would agree with me that that would completely vitiate requirement (B) of the military agreement, the deployment of a company of UNPROFOR soldiers. Those soldiers would have no effect whatsoever in the pocket if basically their military capacity was strangled by the Serbs, would it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot agree with your statement because they were able to conduct activities despite the restrictions that you are talking about, inside the zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm not going to read the evidence out because the Judges have heard it, but there has been extensive evidence in this case of the prevention of the entry of humanitarian aid into the Srebrenica enclave, and it is clear from that evidence that the VRS were behind the prevention of that transit. You would agree with me that if that is correct, then it completely vitiates part (F) of the agreement that humanitarian aid was to continue to be allowed into the city as planned?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I have to answer you bearing in mind the international standards that you are familiar with. There is a very specific requirement that the signatory parties to the demilitarisation agreement that if one signatory party vitiates, violates the agreement, the other one is no longer obliged to comply with it. So if the Muslim side was militarily active, then a number of other elements of the agreement have to be reconsidered because the agreement itself is brought into question. It is no longer a valid agreement. The reason for that was also the conduct and the behaviour of the United Nations forces, which didn't do much to prevent such violations and it was their obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you'll agree with me, General, that part (D) of the agreement was never fulfilled in that the enclave was never properly demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was never fully demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you wish to take a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, Mr. Cayley. This is indeed a convenient time for a break. But maybe it's still a bit too early for our usual lunch break, so let us have a 20-minute break at this point. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, please continue until ten minutes past one, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, we'll work for an hour and ten minutes and then we can both get some lunch. General, I want you now to direct your mind to 1995, so we leave behind us the events of 1992 and 1993, and I want you to now think specifically about Operation Krivaja 95. Now, you said in your evidence that the reason -- one of the reasons for Krivaja 95 was the fact that in June of 1995, there were Muslim infiltrations into Serb units, specifically the Podrinje Brigade, and 40 soldiers were killed. So, infiltrations out of the enclave behind VRS front lines killing Serbian soldiers. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not only there. Also at many other places in the areas of responsibility of the units which were deployed immediately around Srebrenica. I only gave you the most drastic example, but there are quite a few of such examples in my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you also said in your evidence in respect of these infiltration manoeuvres that there is not a single example in the entire war of the VRS making use of the infiltration manoeuvre. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember my exact words, but I will tell you what I think is the truth about that. The VRS did not apply that type of manoeuvre which is often used in these types of wars, whereby it showed that its tactics was that of a defence. I know that there was -- but I know that there was one infiltration manoeuvre in Srebrenica, but it had no military effect whatsoever. I believe that it took place sometime in June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I'll read out exactly what you said, and it can be found at paragraph -- at page number 7822 in the LiveNote transcript so you can refresh your memory. "There is not a single example in the course of the entire war where the army of Republika Srpska made use of this manoeuvre of infiltration, that is to say, infiltrating troops into the rear of the enemy." Now, that's what you said, General. Now, these kinds of infiltration manoeuvres in the -- let me, let me ask you a question. I don't need you to confirm or otherwise. That's in the transcript, what you said. These kinds of manoeuvres involve essentially going to the rear of the enemy, blowing up munition warehouses, artillery storages, killing enemy soldiers. Is that an infiltration manoeuvre, the kind of infiltration manoeuvre that the Muslims were carrying out?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When speaking about infiltration manoeuvre in terms of tactical considerations and tactical doctrine, then that was not the kind of infiltration manoeuvre that is in the question.
