That is the type of activities into the rear of the enemy. When I spoke about the VRS and the fact that they did not make use of infiltration manoeuvre, I was referring to the infiltration of the combat units which would be active from the rear of the enemy and cooperate with the units in the field. That is the kind of manoeuvre I was speaking about. In the doctrine of tactics, it is called "infiltration manoeuvre," and not the other one. But all armies make use of that manoeuvre. The Serb forces did not infiltrate into the rear of the enemy; they simply held the positions. That was their tactics, whereby they showed that they didn't care about taking over the territory which they didn't consider to be theirs in ethnical terms. Maybe I didn't express myself well enough. I wasn't referring to the infiltration of the terrorist group, I just said that the VRS did not make use of the manoeuvre infiltration into the rear of the enemy, and that it did not attempt to take possession of new territories by cooperating with other units in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm not entirely clear now what your point is, so I'll ask you a simple question. Did the Bosnian Serb army ever infiltrate into the rear of Bosnian government forces in order to blow up ammunition storage points, kill enemy soldiers, that sort of thing? Did the Bosnian Serb army ever do that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't testify about that. That was not the kind of a problem that I studied in my research. I just spoke --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Answer that simple question, and I'll state is to you again. It's very clear, as clear as the statement that you made to the courtroom the day before yesterday. Did the Bosnian Serb army ever infiltrate into the rear of Bosnian government forces in order to blow up ammunition storage points, kill enemy soldiers, and that sort of thing? Did the Bosnian Serb army ever do that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I'm not familiar with that fact because I didn't conduct any research in that respect, so I cannot provide you with any answers. And I did not testify about that, and my testimony did not include the kind of activities that you speak about. I testified about the characteristics of the tactics and the tactical doctrine of the VRS. They did not make use of the infiltration manoeuvre in the sense that they would have infiltrated their units, platoons, battalions into the rear of the enemy from where they would attack the units which were along the contact line. That kind of manoeuvre was not used by the VRS, and that is what I spoke about in my testimony. Whether there were cases of infiltration of groups into the rear of the Muslim forces, the groups which would conduct sabotage activities and terrorist activities, I don't know, but I wouldn't be surprised that there were such cases because every -- all armies do that. I wouldn't be surprised to know if -- that the VRS did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could we have Defence Exhibit 149, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, what was the function of the 10th Sabotage Detachment which was, in fact, a unit of the Main Staff? Can you, first of all, point it out for us on the diagram that is in front of you? If you could use the pointer.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the right exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... matter. It's the Main Staff exhibit.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, Madam Registrar, we'll carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're aware that the 10th Sabotage Detachment was a unit of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was their function within the VRS? What was the function of that unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That unit is a so-called detachment. It can be of a company -- that can be a company or a platoon as the nature of their composition. That one was a platoon, which is a rather small unit bearing in mind the general strength of detachments. According to the doctrine that was used by the JNA there were such formations, such temporary formations, but they were usually companies, very often stronger than battalions. This detachment had two platoons --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Don't worry about the size of the unit. I didn't ask you what was the size of the unit. I asked you what is the function. What was the function of the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the name of the unit itself then we can conclude from that name what it was supposed to do. Sabotage or diversionary units are used for sabotage activities into the rear of the enemy including command posts, artillery positions, fire groups, and special reconnaissance assignments. All armies in the world engage in reconnaissance assignments, and one such reconnaissance assignment is to capture members of the enemy army in order to collect intelligence data. That is a common type of behaviour of all armies in the world and that is precisely the role of sabotage detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And all armies in the world, General, engage in infiltration, don't they? And the 10th Sabotage Detachment was an infiltration unit. It was an infiltration unit of the VRS, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, yes. Yes, for the assignments that I spoke about previously, that is to say, for undertaking activities in the rear, the enemy rear, attacking the elements of command and fire support.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, General, I'm not going to read out the evidence to you, but a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment testified before these Honourable Judges and he said exactly that, that the 10th Sabotage Detachment was an infiltration unit used to go behind enemy lines and attack the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is at page 3077, and, Your Honours, that's Mr. Erdemovic testifying to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, based on the fact that you agree with me that the 10th Sabotage Detachment undertook activities in the rear, the enemy rear, attacking elements of the command and fire support, your statement that you said that there is not a single example in the course of the entire war where the army of Republika Srpska made use of this manoeuvre of infiltration, that is completely incorrect, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are interpreting my statement erroneously, Mr. Prosecutor. That is not what I said. What I said was, and let me repeat, when I expounded on the characteristics of the military doctrine of the VRS, I said and I repeat once again that that army did not use infiltration of its forces into the rear of the enemy as a manoeuvre of tactical units on a tactical scale, which means that its battalions and brigades were not infiltrated into the enemy rear in order to have an opposite front and move towards the line of demarcation and work with the forces on the front. That is tactical manoeuvres. But what you're talking about, the kind of infiltration that you are talking about, you are talking about infiltration for the purposes of diversion, sabotage and reconnaissance work, and there is no army in the world which in the tactical and even operative scale does not use that type of activity. That was probably used by the army of Republika Srpska as well. But as I say, I did not speak about that form of activity. I spoke about tactical manoeuvres of turning the front round, upside -- reversing it and joining up with the forces attacking from the front. So that is the kind of manoeuvre that I meant, which is not the same thing as you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, General, what you said yesterday is in the transcript. It's there for everybody to see. I've read it out for the purposes of your cross-examination. I think we can now actually move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Prosecutor's Exhibit 425 could be made available, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a document that we've already discussed. Do you have the Cyrillic version in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you said, in respect of this document and again just so there's no misunderstanding between us about what you've previously said - I think this is at transcript page 7872 - you state that a directive is essentially a list of desirable objectives rather than a strict order. That is how you characterised a directive. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just directives of this type. There are two types of directives. One are prospecting for desirable activity, that is, a forecast for forthcoming activity. Then there are directives which strictly prescribe the operation to be carried out. So these are not executionary directives but directives which serve to plan, forecast, and stipulate what can be expected in the course of the year depending on the period in question. But of course there are directives which are very precise and ones which are very short. Three sentences, for example. And that has to be executed. For example, I know that in 1943, the Supreme Command of the liberation forces of Yugoslavia issued a directive and it was three words, "Prozor must fall," and Prozor did fall. So those directives are executed. So there are other directives which are directives of principle, of forecasting, which must be operisationalised in the operative staff and command to determine what the realistic or what is realistic and feasible under prevailing conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was this directive an order, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So this document has no binding effect; it's not a decision of any kind.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not a decision. It is not a decision for concrete operations. It is just a concept, a conceptual document for the activities in the ensuing year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can just turn to -- I'm not sure which page it is of your version of events. It's paragraph 4. Can you read out the first three words of paragraph 4? Could you read out the first three words of paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Decisive defence in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you're reading actually from the wrong paragraph. Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 says, "The tasks of the Republika Srpska army." Can you read the title out for paragraph 4? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I hereby decide." Is that what you mean? Is that how the paragraph begins? Paragraph 4, "I hereby decide:"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So when Mr. Karadzic wrote "hereby decide," what you're saying he really meant is, "I hereby would like, or hereby would wish that something actually takes place." He wasn't actually making any kind of decision at all.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For you to understand me, you will have to listen to what I say in explanation of this paragraph. Combat documents and documents for command have a certain structure that they follow. In each and every document of command, orders, directives, and so on, there is a fourth point which sets out the conceptual part, the concept, and that is the basic concept from which documents are further elaborated, and plans as well. And just as in the order for the active functioning of the Drina Corps, in paragraph 4 we have the Commander's concept, here too we have the concept of the person issuing the directive, which in this case is the president of Republika Srpska. The president of Republika Srpska availed himself of the structure and dealt with the issues that the directive as an act of command contains. Therefore, within the frameworks of that fourth point or fourth paragraph, he provides a concept. It is the conceptualisation. It is not an absolute order by him that it should be executed. So after this conceptual form we have the elaboration of more concrete forms later on, and then the decision is binding. This decision is still not mandatory, still not binding, and what testifies to that is that the majority of these operations were never, in fact, executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you're a military man. You commanded a battalion. When you commanded your battalion and you made a decision and you expressed that decision to your subordinates, did you expect that decision to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My decision-making was for a day and an hour, not for a year. And strategic bodies give assignments of principle. They -- directive decision making in our terminology means setting out the principles of planning, that is to say, planning in principle of the desirable and possible goals and assignments. And it is up to a concrete analysis of whether that is feasible, and once that question is settled, planning is undertaken. Quite obviously, this particular directive was, in fact, a document of principle which was not compiled as mandatory. Nor was it understood by the Main Staff of the VRS as such, particularly not the cause to which these were intended, that they should prepare and execute them. In this form, the directives were not binding, not mandatory, because for each individual operation, concrete directives were compiled. So this is the concept. This sets out the concept of what should be done but not what must be done on a mandatory basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I apologise for interrupting at this point, but may I say the following. That is, General, the example you quoted, "Prozor must fall," and afterwards you added, "Prozor did fall," what was that, "Prozor must fall"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the directive issued by the supreme command of the national liberation army of Yugoslavia, Josip Broz Tito, in 1943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That means that that authority in a way expressed his will, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it necessary at that level that that particular person had to say Prozor should fall in such and such a way, at what time, what was the date, and so on and so forth with all the specifications? At that level, was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I asked you was, would that same authority, that same individual who said Prozor must fall, should he have had to state the specific time, the way, the manner in which it should fall, the date and so on; or the people who executed this order had to take care of those specific features?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was as you stated, but quite obviously this is not that type of directive. What we have here is not that type of directive, Mr. President, and I endeavoured to indicate the difference between the different types of directives that exist. There are directives which are very concrete and binding, mandatory, and which must be executed; and there are other directives which are directives of principle, plans in principle, and they are not understood as having mandatory power. From this type of directive we go down to the nitty-gritty of working out the particulars, the operations or which parts of this plan should be realised, put into practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. But can we say that the leaders decide by directives, by means of directives?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm still rather confused about the directives, and I asked General Radinovic yesterday about them. It seems still to me that they are more rhetorical than anything else, and we can see them. I mean, I can't imagine a head of state saying I'm going -- I don't know, we have to take that or to take that as we see that happening around us. But how can, how can a General execute this rhetorical order, at what stand? Take even the example, you said, "Prozor must fall." It fell, you said it fell afterwards, but it didn't fall by enchantment, it fell according to a certain plan, clarification, and so on. So the directive is very as -- what can I say, as a policy does not -- it does not surpass the wishful thinking or the preparation of minds. You can see it happening in many parts of the world, a president just conditioning the people. So what is exactly the role of directives here in our field, and the responsibility for it? You don't need to answer me, but I'm still wondering. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer with pleasure. The illustration that I gave to stress the difference between certain types of directives, the operation on Prozor in 1943 was not executed only on the basis of that sentence, "Prozor must fall," but on the basis of that concept by the Supreme Commander, the Main Staff plan, the operation for the liberation of Prozor, and, I might say, in great detail, and so also on the basis of these directives which are the subject of this consideration. For the operation to be implemented, a concrete order is necessary for a concrete time and a concrete area and a concrete unit. And in my testimony, I showed -- I demonstrated that many operations which were planned here and listed here were not implemented at all, were never put into practice. There are no documents to show that anybody was -- held anybody responsible for the operations in this document, that is to say that this type of document was not understood as having to be realised. There is another step after this first step, and that is a concrete order. It would have to have been followed by a concrete order to the units who were supposed to execute them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you also gave evidence, I think the day before yesterday, in respect to the directive, and you stated that the directive did not have a binding nature because there was no obligation on those who received the directive to make reports upwards, back to the initiator of the document. Do you recall saying that or do you want me to read out to you what you said?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I said. I do know what I said. With respect to this directive, I said that as these were documents of principle and not documents which are mandatory to the units to plan an operation, and because there was no call to accountability because -- for the fact that these operations were not indeed carried out and because there were no operative reports that the operations were carried out or not carried out, then for an appraisal of the mandatory character of the directive it was clear that written in this form, in this shape, and according to that programme were not implemented. They were realised on the basis a concretisation, a concrete document based on this document of principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're having difficulty in understanding me, my questions. They're obviously not clear enough for you. So what I'll do is I'll read out your testimony to you and you can either say, "Yes," or "No, I said the following." You stated yesterday: "Those who whom the directive is sent are not obliged to report on the execution of the tasks contained in the directive," and that is at page 7872. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because those assignments were not carried out, and that shows precisely that the doctrine was not binding.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there or was there not a reporting requirement for subordinate units who received this directive?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the doctrinary principle, that an assignment which is carried out or which is assigned -- a task which is assigned must be carried out. That is provided for in the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You misunderstood me General. You misunderstood my question. Did those units who received this directive have an obligation to report to the Supreme Command? Did they have an obligation to report on this order as in any normal military structure where an order is given?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have this obligation because this was not sent as a directive for the execution of an operation. As I said, it was a directive of principle on the assignments that could be executed in the course of the year not which must be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you turn, General, to the final page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could put the final page of this English version of the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now I'm looking at paragraph 7, and I will read it so that there is no misunderstanding between us, General. Paragraph 7 lays out the command and control of the Supreme Command in Pale and then in the third paragraph it states: "Submit reports as follows: "a) regular reports by 1900 hours with situation as at 1700 hours. "b) interim reports as the need arises and in the case of surpise action or incursions by the enemy. "c) reports on readiness for offensive operations. "d) summary reports every third day during active combat operations." So the fact is, General, is in fact the subordinate units or the subordinate unit who received this directive did have an obligation to respond to the Supreme Command as with any normal military order, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, answer the question. Did the units that received this directive have an obligation to respond? Did they have an obligation to respond to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this directive, no, but to the directives that they were to receive and which relate to them particularly for the execution of concrete operations. In this directive, as you know, Krivaja 95, it relates to the Hercegovina Corps and the valley of the river Neretva and not to Krivaja 95, which was performed in the Srebrenica region. Therefore, it is not natural that the Hercegovina Corps report on the Krivaja operation, although it has been mentioned here. But it did not perform that operation. So point 7, paragraph 7, is a point which must exist in each act of command, and the person issuing the act knows that it is a component part of that item -- that a component part of that item 7 is that reports be submitted and the deadlines for that be stipulated but for operations which are carried out, not for operations which are not carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There is a reporting obligation, isn't there, in this directive, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what is carried out, but not as an answer to this directive but to the directives which stipulate the execution of concrete operations in a concrete space of time and a concrete area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on, General. And again, I can quote your testimony back to you if there is any disagreement about what you said or didn't say. Do you recall yesterday stating that: "There is no operative link between directive 7 and 7/1," which is the Main Staff document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 426 [sic], Mr. Usher. If that can be made available to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "There is no link between those two documents, 7 and 7/1, and the operation Krivaja 95." Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I meant Krivaja 95, which was carried out by the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to page 10 of the English version. I think it's page 8 in your version. Can you go to the final sentence of the first paragraph, and the paragraph is headed up "Drina Corps." Do you see the paragraph "Drina Corps"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's page 10, Mr. Usher, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you see that, General, where it says "Drina Corps"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you read the sentence which begins "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text here, "Drina Corps." If we have the same text: "By extremely persistent and active defence in the north-western part of the war front and around the enclaves, prevent enemy breakthroughs along --"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I'll read it out. It's the final sentence of the first paragraph, and actually, I can see it quite clearly in the Cyrillic there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I'm sorry to interrupt you. What document are you referring to, 426?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 425. I'm sorry if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we read on the record 426. There is a problem here because we cannot follow it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's 425.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Actually, that was my fault. I actually -- I do want that document. I want that document ready but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, it's page 10 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Page 10 in the English, and I believe it's page 8 in the Serbian version. General, I'll read out -- it's the final two sentences, actually, of the first paragraph. Actually, the final sentence of the first paragraph moving into the second paragraph: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." The next sentence: "In case UNPROFOR leaves, UNPROFOR forces leave Zepa and Srebrenica, the Drina Corps Command shall plan an operation named Jadar with the task of breaking up and destroying the Muslim forces in these enclaves and definitively liberating the Drina valley region." Now, in respect of the first sentence that I read out, "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations," that is a directive to eliminate the enclave of Srebrenica, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there is disagreement between the directive of the Main Staff, which is directly superior to the Corps Commanders, and the directives which was issued by the president of the republic as the Superior Commander of the Main Staff. So the first level of responsibility in commanding the VRS is the Supreme Commander, and we showed this on the illustration, on the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry to interrupt you but again you must have misunderstood my question. What I'm asking you is would any sensible military officer interpret that sentence to mean the elimination of the enclave at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This directive is not an execution directive. I showed that and I'm telling you this today. Directive 7 is not an execution directive after that. It should be followed by directives from the Main Staff. Then there is directive 7 -- then there are directives which should follow up directive 7, develop it. So the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think Mr. Cayley read to the witness two sentences and now he's asking him, as I see -- well, the question is: "Would any officer interpret that sentence to mean the elimination of the enclave at Srebrenica." I don't know whether he meant both sentences or just one. So perhaps this could clarify -- this could be clarified for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I referred him to the first sentence actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I think that the Prosecutor's question was quite clear. I'm going to quote it in English. [In English] "What I'm asking you is would any sensible military officer interpret that sentence to mean the elimination of the enclave at Srebrenica?" So put you in the place of this military officer and interpret this, even if you are going to make an operational directive or order. Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please give us direct answers.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First officer which received -- who received this directive is the Commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, and for that very reason, because he would interpret that sentence in the way that Mr. Cayley is asking and that you are asking, Your Honour, he knew its meaning, and in his directive which he issued, and that is directive 7/1, there is no such sentence. This sentence doesn't appear. Thereby he expresses his disagreement with that sentence, and that sentence was left out of directive 7/1, which was closer, actually, to the corps system, to the system of the corps which was supposed to carry out the directive. So this sentence is not contained in directive 7/1. So this directive does have this sentence, and the other one does not contain that sentence for the very reason that the sense, the meaning, of that sentence was understood by that officer, and it was left out of the text of directive 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So General, you would agree with General Dannatt's assessment of this order when he stated in respect of this particular portion of the directive that we're discussing, he said, "Well I think what is intended here is that Srebrenica and Zepa should be captured, and I would assume that the reference to `no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa' meant that not only were those towns to be captured, but that the existing population should be removed from those places." Now, based on what you've just said to the president, you agree with that assessment of this particular portion of the directive?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could move on to Prosecutor's Exhibit 426. Now, General, you have stated to the Judges already that there is no mention of directive 7 in this order, that is, Exhibit 426, the directive of the Main Staff. Do you confirm that testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That directive 7 is not mentioned. To tell you the truth, I don't recall saying that, that it is not mentioned, but that it cannot in the sense of directive for the execution of actions --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, before it disappears off the transcript, let me repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me repeat your answer to the president. "Thereby he expresses his disagreement with that sentence and that sentence was left out of directive 7/1." That is what you have just said to the Court.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, I said that. So that there is no sentence that you quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think Mr. Cayley's question was not interpreted correctly to the witness, so perhaps that is the cause of the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Visnjic, yes, if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's confirm, General. You state, stated in your evidence that there is no mention of directive 7 in the Main Staff document directive 7/1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say that. I said that that sentence from directive 7 that you quoted is not mentioned. It is not contained in directive 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that directive 7 is incorporated by reference in directive 7/1, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because it is a document that has a more general -- higher level of generality, so it is in a way a plan of task, so it is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 4 in the English version. In fact, page 2 in the English version, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could move that into the centre of the screen, Mr. Usher. Could you move it down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, paragraph 2 outlines the tasks of the VRS, and it states, "On the basis of directive number 7, the VRS has the task," and then it outlines all of the tasks that have to be fulfilled. Now, you would agree with me that that is an incorporation of directive 7 by reference into this document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, relying on it or mentioning it, yes, but in the strict adherence to each formulation, no, and that this is -- the fact that this is true is proved by the fact that the sentence on the elimination of enclaves from directive 7 was eliminated in this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now if you could go to page 4, and it's paragraph 4. Now, General, this is a document signed by Colonel-General Ratko Mladic, the Commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, and in paragraph 4 he states "I have decided." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then if you go down to the bottom of your page, the last paragraph, "Other forces of the VRS shall contribute to the conduct of operations Sadejstvo 95 with the goal of operative strategic camouflage and correcting the operative tactical position," and this is the important part, General, "by carrying out planned combat, battles and operations in accordance with directive number 7 and active combat operations towards Bugojno, Travnik, Kladanj, Olovo and Vares and around the Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde enclaves in the Bihac pocket." So it's correct, isn't it, General, that General Mladic was directly referencing directive 7 in respect of the Srebrenica enclave; he was incorporating by direct reference the language of Mr. Karadzic in directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it was not incorporated by reference because in this paragraph that you read from, General Mladic's directive, elimination of the enclaves is not mentioned, but active -- activities or action around the enclaves is mentioned. So action or elimination is not the same linguistically, semantically, and particularly not from the aspect of consequences of such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, General, that when General Mladic wrote this order in respect of combat operations towards Srebrenica, he had directive 7 in his mind; otherwise, he wouldn't have written it down here, would he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I agree with that. He did have it in mind, but he corrected its aspirations, particularly having in mind the consequences which would ensue if he had accepted that sentence which is contained in directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, in your evidence yesterday you stated that the fact that there was no mention of directive number 7, Karadzic document, in directive 7/1 indicated a certain duality of command. Now, you would agree with me that I've now shown you two direct references to that document, that your theory of duality based on the fact that 7 was not mentioned in 7/1 is completely false?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I do not agree with what you say. I think that this directive shows that this duality, rivalry exists, and this duality will result in a major clash between the political leadership of Republika Srpska and the Main Staff of VRS in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, General Mladic is saying in this document on two occasions, "on the basis of directive number 7"; "in accordance with directive number 7." If he is acting on the basis of "in accordance" with something, he is following those orders, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he's correcting them so as not to speculate. I showed you in a direct example that he has significantly corrected the directive of the president of the republic by not accepting to eliminate the enclaves, only to carry out activities around the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, but the directive 7 was public. It was known also by the other officers or generals. So would they in applying directive 7/1, would they also take into consideration directive 7 the way you would take into consideration the law when you apply, for instance, a regulation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the directive is a state secret; it's not a public document. It only goes or is transmitted along a strict command system to only a certain number of senior officers. In directive 7/1, it is very clear -- it is clearly shown that the Main Staff of the VRS, in the face of its Commander who signed directive 7/1, does not accept the expression nor the intention of the sentence contained in directive 7 but significantly modifies it, thus indicating that there was a dual competence or authority in the military system, because -- as has been shown, this was good because directive 7/1 is more in compliance with international norms and the agreement on the demilitarisation and the safe zones than directive 7. So as a military expert, this was an indication to me which showed that there were differences, and that the system of the functioning of the VRS did not proceed along strictly hierarchical principles which would be natural in any army in the world. It is one weakness of that system which, in certain stages and periods, deviated from this which disrupted relations and also the efficacy of that system. So this is something which we can see that is evident when you compare directive 7 and directive 7/1. So it's not natural to expect the Main Staff of the VRS to completely ignore a directive of the Supreme Commander. Of course, this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is not natural. So he refers to that directive in order to give some legal basis for the things that he is doing in his own directive, but it's obvious that he significantly changes it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Before I -- thank you. But once you refer to it, isn't it a fact that you are adopting it in the eyes of those who will execute later? They know that there is -- that 7/1 has got its source in directive 7, and they are legitimately entitled to apply them, to apply both. Is that logical if you were applying it, not analysing it as a professor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only -- no, Your Honour. The logic of military activity is to execute the orders of the immediate superiors because this order would be derived from the secondary superior officer, because usually orders are carried out from the immediately preceding level. And here it is obvious that the Main Staff did not adhere to everything or did not carry out everything that the president of the republic, i.e., the Supreme Commander, asked them to do; and I think this is a good thing, rather than apply or execute this order literally because of the consequences of such an act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But would they be responsible or accountable if they applied also the supreme order or this gives them green light to apply it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the green light is given. I don't think that the green light has been given because the Commander of the Main Staff has excluded that from his own document, meaning that this is not something that he is ordering, this task to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, when the Srebrenica enclave was eliminated in July of 1995, who was the Commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Commander of the Main Staff was General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can carry on if you wish, Mr. President. Yes. If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 427, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, this is the preparatory order for operation Krivaja 95. You can see it's signed by -- this edition, version, is not signed but it is a document that is from General Zivanovic. Could you read out, please, from paragraph 2 up to and including the words "Main Staff." You can stop at the words "Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, General. The paragraph that's numbered 2.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Drina Corps Command," "The Command of the Drina Corps"? Is that the one that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What document does the witness have in front of him, 427?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 of that document, General, if you could read that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the past three months, the enemy started and is still conducting --"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's numbered 2, General. I can see what you're doing. It's the secdon -- I'll read it out for you if it's a problem. Paragraph 2 reads: "Based on directives OP numbers 7 and 7/1 of Republika Srpska army Main Staff," and then the order carries on and gives more detail. This preparatory order, General, was based, was it not, on directive 7 from the Supreme Staff and directive 7/1 from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my testimony that is what I was talking about and that is what I said on several occasions. The operation Krivaja 95 was planned on the basis of what you have just read, including also the phrase "and the current situation." And the situation in the month of July was such that the Commander of the corps had to plan and execute such an operation, and I testify and I abide by what I have said. I really cannot answer the question as to what exactly constituted the basis for the planning of the operation because in both directive 7 and directive 7/1, Krivaja refers to a completely different area. It refers to the area of the Neretva River valley which is a different part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it concerns the Herzegovinian Corps and not the Drina Corps, and it was on the basis of that that I concluded that the operation indeed was not planned or executed based on directives number 7 and 7/1 but on the basis of the current situation. And there must have been a different act of command, a different document whereby the operation would be launched. In my research, I didn't come across such a document, but I am certain that it existed because the operation could not be planned and conducted on the basis of what it says here, directives 7 and 7/1, because the location in question in directives number 7 and 7/1 is completely different and it pertains to a different area. So there cannot be any link on the basis of which you can say that these two directives constituted the basis for the planning of the Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you accept now that when you said that there was no operative link between 7 and 7/1 and these orders in respect of Krivaja 95 that that position is erroneous based on what the documents themselves say?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you accept now that what you said previously about the linkage between document 7 and 7/1 and the Krivaja 95 orders is incorrect? Let me read back to you just to remind the Court what you said yesterday. "I can find no link between directives 7 and 7/1 and the order for Krivaja 95." Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I still stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on to the final document, General, which is 428.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, perhaps we can do it after the break. We shall now have a 50-minute break and come back at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's 428, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 428.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, let's -- I'll just remind you where we were before the break, when you had confirmed to me that you could find no linkage between document 7 and 7/1 and the Krivaja 95 order, and you confirmed that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If page three of the English version can be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And General, if you would go to paragraph 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the reference of the Court, this is the final order for Krivaja 95 dated the 2nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have paragraph 2 to hand, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you read paragraph 2, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to operations directive number 7 and 7/1 of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and on the basis of the situation in the Corps area of responsibility, has the task of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone, as soon as possible, in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, and to reduce them to their urban areas."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then, General, if you could go to paragraph 4 just below there where it states, I think, about five or six lines down, "Objective: By surprise attack." Could you read that out to the Court.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could. "Objective of the option: By a surprise attack to separate and reduce in size the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, to improve the tactical position of the forces in the depth of the area, and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So General, would you agree with me that the principal purposes of the Operation Krivaja 95 was, one, to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica; two, to reduce them to their urban areas; three, to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 425, page 10 of the English version, page 8 of the Serb version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cayley. Was there anywhere some kind of explanation of the word "elimination" of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There's no elaboration, Your Honour. I'll simply read it to you: "... and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You can't raze them out of the planet, so what does the meaning of elimination is -- what is the meaning of "elimination," just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm going to read to you from Mr. Karadzic's document, which is directive number 7, the first document that we started with today, and he states halfway down that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you not found it yet, Mr. Usher? Sorry, it's page 10 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, do you have it in front of you? It's page 8.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm reading halfway down the paragraph titled "Drina Corps." "Using operational and tactical camouflage measures while in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. Secondly, by planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Now, General, if we go back to General Zivanovic's order, paragraph 2, you agree with me that he was stating that one of the objectives of Krivaja 95 was to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, and you would agree with me that that is exactly what Radovan Karadzic is directing in directive 7, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the other condition that General Zivanovic was laying down in his order was to create conditions for the elimination of the enclave, and I think you would agree with me that creating an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa is, in fact, creating conditions for the elimination of the enclave, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that is not so, looking at it from the military point of view. Speaking in military terms, creating conditions for the elimination of the enclaves implies taking possession of the key features around the enclave and, if necessary, for the separation of the enclaves to be carried out. However, in the order issued by General Zivanovic, there is no such instruction for the elimination of the enclave. There is no such order. Had that been the objective, he would have ordered it. He would have ordered the elimination of the enclaves, which he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, can you answer Judge Riad's question? What does "eliminate" mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the order issued by the Drina Corps Commander, such a phrase cannot be found but the phrase to create conditions for the elimination of the enclave. Again, in military terms, it would mean to have the forces actually enter the enclave and take possession of all the key facilities, which would mean that the VRS would thereby establish control over the enclave; that is, the enclave would no longer exist as such. It would not exist as a term. It would no longer be the base of the army, and it could no longer be controlled by the Muslim army. Such an objective was not set out in the order. That task was not defined. It would have been -- the combat disposition would have been completely different had that been the objective, and that was not the objective of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But that is exactly what the VRS did and completed, by your testimony, by July the 10th, 1995, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but prior to that, both the population and the military had left the enclave and the area would already be completely empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just ask, General, because I understand that an army would say taking possession of the enclave, but eliminating a part of a country, does that include also its people?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elimination of the enclave implies eliminating those conditions and those factors which set out that area as a different area -- distinct area within the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps. In that region, in that part of the enclave, there were both military and civilian authorities that were in place which were not controlled by the VRS. The elimination of the enclave would imply that a military and political control had to be established over that area. It does not imply the forcible removal of the population or the destruction of property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, just to follow up this reasoning, the enclave is eliminated not because it is the wrong place geographically, it is distinct you say. It is a distinct area. It is distinct because of its people. That's the only distinction.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also because of the authorities and because of the military which was there. But here in this case primarily because of the military, because of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So just eliminate the soldiers and not the people. That's the order "elimination," in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The elimination of the enclave, militarily speaking, does not imply expelling the population or any violence against the population. It implies a military victory over the forces which control the area, the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When it is accompanied by this making it impossible or difficult for them to stay, doesn't this throw a new light and show that this elimination includes the people too?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I testified to the effect that that sentence cannot be found in 7/1. The command of the Main Staff left it out, and in that sense, the Drina Corps did not have that obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Even as a background?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, do you have your report to hand?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page 28 of your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have this other version. I think it will be easier for me if you just tell me what it is that you want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'd like you to read -- is that the -- that's the original language. Page 28, please, General, paragraph 3.1. Could you read the first sentence, in fact the first two sentences of paragraph 3.1 on page 28.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the Drina Corps Operation Srebrenica was code named Krivaja 95. It was based on the directives of the president of Republika Srpska and the Commander of the army Main Staff." Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. And you stand by that statement in your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by it; however, with the caveat that I expressed during my testimony, that is, that it was essentially based on the analysis of the situation in the month of June and the activities of the Muslim forces in the rear of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you'd agree with me in the next sentence of your report you actually state that the assessment of the situation in Middle Podrinje is contained in those directives. The assessment which you're referring to is based on the directives themselves, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the assessment, but also on the assessments that they made themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me read, General, to the Court so it's in the record what you actually do say in that paragraph. "In these directives," and this is paragraph 3.1 on page 28, "In these directives it was assessed that the situation in Middle Podrinje could become complicated if the status quo persisted; that is, if the area between the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa stayed under Muslim control, and the forces of the 28th Infantry Division from both enclaves remained active. On the basis of this assessment of the situation, Drina Corps Commander was ordered to prevent at all costs the penetration of the forces of the Muslim 2nd Corps along the routes leading from Tuzla and Kladanj towards the area of Srebrenica and to urgently separate the two enclaves and occupy the area between them with his forces, that is, to separate the enclaves and reduce them to the borders of the safe areas as established by the agreement signed in April and May of 1993." And you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me just read to you the few lines of the next paragraph. "Recognising," this is paragraph 3.2, "Recognising the Muslim intentions after having successfully broken the Muslim offensive in the direction of Tuzla and Kladanj on June 24, 1995, and neutralised nine sabotage terrorist groups infiltrated in the wider region of Han Pijesak and Vlasenica on June 26, 1995, and in accordance with the assignments given in directives number 7 and 7/1 on July 2nd, 1995, the Drina Corps started immediate preparations for the execution of the operation," and then you go on to explain the Srebrenica, the Krivaja 95, operation. Do you stand by that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do, because mention is made here of sabotage and terrorist groups which were nine in total at the end of June, and that was the reason for the planning of the operation, the immediate reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, do you recall yesterday, changing subject slightly, that you said that for the Drina Corps Commander to have a mandate to issue orders to MUP forces, he would have to have had authority from the Main Staff. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that is applicable to all units which are not part of his formation, including MUP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you clarified it by saying that there would have to be some indication that the Drina Corps had been given the capacity to order an MUP unit for a particular task and for a particular time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you state -- you stated in your evidence that you've seen absolutely no evidence at all to indicate that the Drina Corps had such authority?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the MUP unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which was effective on the road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, General. Have you seen any evidence to suggest that the Drina Corps had been given this kind of authority?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, could you just have a look at paragraph 3.8 of your report. It's on page 30 in your version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, it's page 31. I'm sorry, page 30 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you find it, General? I think it's around 30 or 31 - your pagination is different to mine - and it deals with all the assignments of the units.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the units, it's on page 29 in my version, if it is paragraph 3.8 that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you go to the final paragraph where it refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, Mr. Cayley, but the document that we have on the ELMO is not that report. I think you're thinking about -- that you're talking about paragraph 3.8, and is it page 30, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's very confusing, because the problem is there are two different English versions with two different numbering systems and then there's a Serbian version also with a different numbering system and that's where the confusion arises. In fact, the section that's on the ELMO is correct. I'll keep a close eye on it to make sure that we have the right page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you'd raise it, Mr. Usher. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, can you read the last paragraph of that section which begins "The Skelani," and you can stop after the word "reserve."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Skelani Independent Battalion, in the role of Corps' reserve."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, can you explain on what basis you made that statement? And I assume that you made that statement -- you're saying that the Skelani Battalion was allocated as the reserve for Krivaja 96, for the operation Krivaja 95? Can you explain how you came to that conclusion? It's not. What is it the reserve for, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Skelani Battalion was part of the organic composition of the Drina Corps. It was not attached to it but was within the composition of the Drina Corps, and the Corps Commander decided not to engage that battalion in the first echelon but to leave it in reserve, to leave it in reserve with the assignment of possible action which could ensue with the development of events if the need arose. If there was a lag in the advance of its units -- of his units, then the Corps Commander could use this to improve the operative situation along the axis where the need was -- where this was required. That is the role of a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, how do you come to the conclusion that the Skelani Battalion was allocated by the Drina Corps Commander as the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By studying the documents that I had at my disposal and by reconstructing the combat disposition. Therefore, it was my duty to set forth how the actions at Srebrenica followed on from each other within the Krivaja 95 operation, which implied that I had to identify the first echelon for active combat activities and the second echelon or a possible reserve depending on which forces were utilised. I concluded, on the basis of my studies and research, on the basis of the analysis of the relevant documents, that the Skelani Battalion was a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you identify for the Judges which documents you relied on to come to the conclusion that the Skelani Battalion was the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of a number of documents, documents which I had at my disposal. And I also had studies of an internal nature which were used in the high military schools and academies, and on the basis of my own personal contacts with the participants in the operation. So it was on the basis of all that material that I deduced that the Skelani Battalion was a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see in any documents that you were provided by the Defence the Skelani Battalion named as the Reserve Battalion during operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure at this point whether I saw that in the documents provided to me by the Defence, but quite certainly I did find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, do you have Prosecutor's Exhibit 428 before you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Does the General have 428? Or if he hasn't, could he be given it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, do you have the version in your own language of Krivaja 95 before you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have it in front of you now, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You see the first paragraph in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, so there's no confusion, this is the operative order for Krivaja 95 that we're referring to signed by General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's addressed to the commands of various units within the Drina Corps. Is the Skelani Battalion referred to at all in that address block?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not referred to, to whom it is sent, and I came to the conclusion that the Skelani Battalion was in reserve and that it got into that position on the basis of the studies which I had at my disposal in the centre of high military schools. There is a graduate study that was done there and the topic of it was the Srebrenica operation at the war school, and it expressly states that the Skelani Battalion was a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If need be, if that is absolutely necessary, I could find the document and you can check that out. I didn't quote it because it wasn't a public source.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, let's go to page 3 of this combat order, to the bottom of the page, and you'll see there that the order, like all normal combat orders, refers to the reserve force. Can you read to the Judges what this order says about reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Reserve forces, three to four forces of the MUP and one company from the Vlasenica, Vlasenica Brigade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but there seems to be some confusion. Could the usher place on the ELMO the document that you are reading so that three parties can follow. So that the interpreters can follow, number one; so that the Judges can follow, number two; and the public in the public gallery, number 3. And I would like to appeal to the technical booth that when we analyse and read a document, could they focus on the text so that the public gallery can see it on the screen. So those are three very good reasons, Mr. Cayley, to state the page and paragraph of the document so that the usher can place it on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. It's page 5. Perfect. And I'll read it so that there's no uncertainty. "Reserve forces of a size of two or three companies of the Ministry of the Interior and one company from the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade. Task: to be in readiness to launch an attack in order to strengthen the force and enhance the success along the battalion's axes of attack; to repel an enemy counter-attack; to secure our hold on the features on the lines reached; to prevent an enemy withdrawal; to secure the flanks and the rear of the attacking forces, and other tasks."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you would agree with me, General, that these two or three companies of the Ministry of the Interior and the one company of the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade were in fact the reserve forces for Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The companies that are mentioned of the MUP are the forces of the local police which absolutely have no combat potential of a company. And in studying the documents for this operation, I doubted, to tell you the truth, whether it was forces that could carry out this operation, and I sought out what was in the reserve. And studying the material, I came to the conclusion that it must have been the Skelani battalion and not these companies because they were local police forces which did not have the combat strength to act as a reserve in the sense of this document here. And that is why my statement in my expert report is different from this order, for the simple reason that the local police forces were not intended to carry out these assignments. And any other police forces, for them to be able to be deployed, the Brigade Commander must have authorisation to issue them assignments, and the doctrinary principle which must not be infringed upon with regard to the use of forces attached is that they must not be split up but must be deployed as a whole. So you cannot divide up an attached unit. That is a doctrinary principle, and this principle must not be infringed upon according to our doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And being fully aware of that particular principle, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you at that point, General. Would you agree with me that the reserve forces are being given a combat assignment by the Corps Commander on the basis of this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you're suggesting to the Judges that General Zivanovic, in full knowledge of the capacities of the local police, was giving a combat instruction to a unit that he knew had no ability to carry out any kind of combat operation at all, on your theory of these units being the local police force?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know full well that those police forces haven't got the power and strength to carry out that assignment. What General Zivanovic ordered at that time, I don't know; I know what he wrote. And I do know that the forces that he determined as a reserve were not sufficient to carry out an operation -- an assignment of that kind. And so I sought out fresh elements which are not contained in the order itself, because in this order, the Skelani Battalion is lost. It's not there, and therefore I assume that it was the Skelani Battalion which was the reserve force. And this was borne out by a graduate report by an officer of the Republika Srpska army and his graduate thesis, and he expressly states that the Skelani Battalion was the reserve force in this operation. And, as I said a moment ago, I can send that in as an additional document for you to see for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I apologise, I have to interrupt again. General, are you saying at this point that the Skelani Battalion was able to accomplish the tasks that these two or three companies were to have done according to the order, pursuant to the order? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say is -- I want to say two things. First of all, that these MUP companies were not capable of carrying out that assignment, and second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood correctly -- but perhaps I didn't understand you. What I understood was that you were saying that these forces could not have been the reserve forces, but you conclude that the Skelani Battalion was the reserve force; is that correct? Am I right in understanding that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that the Skelani Battalion was the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is yes or no, right. So what I understood is correct. Now I'm asking you the following: Did you know what the dimensions and characteristics were of the Skelani Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know that the Skelani Battalion was composed of elderly persons, predominately? Did you have that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was a combat unit. The Skelani Battalion was a combat unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at all events, the information that I have now is that the Skelani Battalion was composed predominately of elderly persons and that it was a provisional battalion; and after the assignment, there was talk of its dissolution. Now, with all these characteristic features of that battalion, could it carry out the task of these two or three companies, even if they were MUP companies, that is to say, police companies? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP companies were not units for combat activities within the combat disposition of military units. They were there to secure the territory, to control the territory, and to implement additional assignments with the frameworks of the combat disposition of the units, and that the Commanders of the units had to unite them when they were in their zone. And assignments are not given, combat assignments are not given to MUP companies. They're not capacitated for those aassignments, nor are they equipped for them, because they are the classical type of police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. You have answered my question. Now please continue responding to the questions put to you by Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could -- do you still have page 3 in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you go to the top of page 3, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the usher could move the page down. Actually, it's page 4, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, could you read paragraph 2 on page 3? It's the fifth line down.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The 2nd Battalion to be formed from the part of the forces of the 1st Birac and 2nd Romanija Brigade were a company from the Skelani Independent Infantry Battalion." Do you want me to continue reading.
