utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You'd agree with me, General, that in fact the Skelani Battalion was not the reserve force, and in fact, it was a component of the 2nd Battalion allocated for combat operations during Krivaja 95, from what you've just read, your own words?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In military terminology, when sections are taken away from some units and attached to another, the unit retains its name. So the Skelani Battalion was still called the Skelani battalion, regardless of the fact that one company was attached by the Commander to another battalion for active -- for action. It has not disappeared; it is just weakened by that one company which has been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But bearing in mind, General, that the people who drafted these documents were professional, sensible people - in fact, General Krstic himself was involved in the planning of this operation - don't you think that if part of the Skelani Battalion, that was not in the 2nd Battalion, had been allocated for the reserve forces, he would have actually expressed that in this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It needn't be. The 2nd Battalion remains. No, that is to say that the Skelani Battalion retains its title, its name, regardless of having been weakened in this fashion. This need not be stated, but the person taking over command responsibility, to be able to take over that responsibility, must be told.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So one company from the Skelani Battalion does actually receive an express written order, and the other part, which is part of the reserve forces, doesn't receive any written order at all from the Corps Commander. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not my evidence. I have tried to answer this in response to your previous question. The reserve of the forces named here by the Corps Commander on page 3 in his order for active combat action, according to me, is not sufficient and is not capable for that type of action. It is not a combat unit. It is a police unit which is not intended for that action. That told me that I ought to seek out the actual forces which were the reserve force of the corps for this operation because the Corps Commander would not carry out any operation without a reserve force, and a reserve force can be two battalions, one battalion, a weakened battalion, but it cannot be without a reserve force for carrying out assignments which can be needed within the course of an operation. In seeking this out, I tried to reconstruct the operative system of the corps and arrived at the fact that the Skelani Battalion was the reserve force without that one company, minus that one company which was attached to someone else. So that is not unusual. It is nothing unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, it's --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the use of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, it's ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous B/S/C translation continues] ... interpretation at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We're not getting the -- I think it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, it's unusual, isn't it, that the Skelani Battalion got no notification that there was no reserve force during this operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally feel that it was stated but by mistake it wasn't written down here, because I can only assume that the officer that wrote his graduate thesis at the high school, high military school in the Yugoslavia army, that he was well-informed. I don't know what post he held, but quite simply, I think it is rather a mistake or an omission in the text than -- because it was quite certain that the battalion was a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, what part of the MUP was actually capable of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single part of MUP is meant to conduct combat actions because --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, have you heard of the Special Brigade of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what is their task?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their task is to carry out special police assignments, special police assignments. The doctrine of police tasks is not in my area of expertise so I didn't really study that, but I do know that police forces are not used --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General. General, does the Special Brigade of the MUP have a combat capacity?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Special Brigade of the MUP did have combat capacity but it is not a unit which is meant for and which is used for combat assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you're in agreement with me that General Zivanovic, in this order, is giving a combat assignment to a MUP unit, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which MUP unit are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The MUP unit that's referred to in this order, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are some local MUP forces. They are not used in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you're not answering my question so I'll put it to you again. You're in agreement with me, aren't you, that General Zivanovic, in this order, is giving a combat assignment to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zivanovic, the local police forces, which were on the territory, could have -- General Zivanovic could have considered them forces which would be able to perform some of the tasks in respect of the combat control of the territory. So they could guard facilities, they could carry out patrols, and so on. So in that sense, they could be reserve forces but not as combat forces because these are not formations which are intended for these purposes. He himself knows that they are not able to carry that out, and I'm sure that General Zivanovic would not issue such an assignment to units of the local forces, to any police forces because police forces are not meant to carry out combat operations. They are intended for police assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that the task issued to the reserve forces here is in fact a combat assignment? And before you answer, General, let me read it to you so there is no misunderstanding. "To be in readiness to launch an attack." That's a combat assignment, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a combat assignment. It's a task of the reserve which is carried out by reserves by definition. But these MUP forces cannot carry out such an assignment, and I'm quite sure that he did not mean the MUP forces but he meant the forces of the Skelani Battalion. And these companies of the local police were ready or in readiness to carry out police assignments in the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, a defence witness has stated to the Judges that General Zivanovic was not present at the forward command post in Pribicevac until at least the 10th of July of 1995. Now, we know that General Krstic was present at the forward command post from on or about the 6th of July of 1995. Now, based on your theory that in the absence of the Corps Commander the Chief of Staff is the deputy Commander, would you agree with me that General Krstic was, in fact, in command of operation Krivaja 1995 from the 6th to the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with you because I have no reliable indicators where General Zivanovic was. But regardless of that, regardless of the fact where General Zivanovic was at that time, the Corps Commander who carried out the operation Krivaja 95 was General Zivanovic. There is no document based on which that Commander is excluded. And he, according to his own personal assessment, could have been in any part of the area of responsibility including the forward command post but also in the north-west of the area of responsibility, in the region of activity of the 1st Zvornik Brigade, i.e., the Bircani Brigade which was holding the front towards Tuzla. So this would be in the competency and within the rights of the Corps Commander to find himself or to be at any moment at the place he felt was a priority place at that point in time. When the Commander is not there, automatically the command duty is assumed by his deputy, i.e., the Chief of Staff. If General Zivanovic was not there at that time of course Krstic was carrying out the command, but this does not rule out the command competencies of the Commander. So Krstic was the Chief of Staff, and in that role he always substitutes for the Commander when the Commander is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was in command of Krivaja 95 from the 6th of July to the 10th of July, 1995? Just give me a name, General. Just give me name. Who was in command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Commander of the Corps was in command of the forces in the Zepa [as interpreted] operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had the command responsibility towards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I either think that we have a lapse or a mistake in the transcript because we're talking about operation Srebrenica and not operation Zepa, as it states in page 95, line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in line 4 as well, I think. We will have to check the record, Mr. Cayley. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's in the response of the witness, Your Honour. He says the Commander of the Corps was in command of the forces in the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You meant the Srebrenica operation, didn't you, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. You said from the 6th to the 10th. That is not Zepa. We're talking about the Srebrenica operation, from the 6th to the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's fine, General. You've corrected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you wish to go on any further or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Mr. Cayley. I think that we should adjourn at this point. It is 3.00. We will continue tomorrow at 9.20. The Chamber has other commitments to fulfil, so we have to call it a day at this point. Have a good afternoon, and I will see you again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
